name: Sundararaja Perumal Temple, Anbil
deity: Vishnu as Sundararaja Perumal (Vadivazhagiya Nambi), reclining, with the Goddess Azhagiyavalli — the handsome lord on the Kollidam bank
period: A Divya Desam of the Chola country, sung by Thirumazhisai Alvar in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham
summary: On the bank of the Kollidam at Anbil, Vishnu reclines as Sundararaja Perumal, the handsome Vadivazhagiya Nambi, with Azhagiyavalli Thayar — a Chola-country Divya Desam sung by Thirumazhisai Alvar.

sections.history: Anbil lies on the northern bank of the Kollidam, east of Lalgudi in the Tiruchirappalli district, and the place is also remembered by the old names Mandukapuri and Brahmapuri. It is one of the 108 Divya Desams in Chola Nadu, sung by Thirumazhisai Alvar in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham. The temple is believed to have been raised by the Cholas in the later eighth century, and the Anbil copper plates preserve the memory of Chola generosity to the village. Anbil was also the home of Aniruddha Brahmarayar, the minister of the Chola king Sundara Chola. The temple is administered today by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department.
sections.architecture: The sanctum stands under the Tharaka Vimanam, and the temple tank is the Manduka Theertham, named for the frog (manduka) of the old place name. Sundararaja Perumal reclines in bhujanga sayanam, with his two consorts holding his feet in such a way that the feet are hidden from view — a rare detail in the iconography of the reclining Lord. Azhagiyavalli Thayar has her own shrine. The temple follows the Dravidian manner of the Chola country.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells that Brahma, proud of his power of creation, was cursed by Vishnu to be born on earth. Repenting, he came to Anbil, prayed to the Lord here and was relieved of the curse; hence the place is called Brahmapuri. The Lord is known as Vadivazhagiya Nambi, the one of beautiful form, a name that gives the temple its tender character.
sections.festivals: The best-known festival is the Theerthavari of the month of Masi, in February–March, when the Lord is taken in procession to the water. Vaikunta Ekadashi is also observed with devotion. Confirm festival dates locally, as they follow the Tamil almanac.
sections.experience: A tranquil riverside Divya Desam away from the busier shrines of the Cauvery delta. Look for the hidden feet of the reclining Lord, walk around the Manduka Theertham, and pause to remember that this is the land of Aniruddha Brahmarayar. It combines well with a visit to Srirangam or Lalgudi.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan sessions and a midday closure; Vaikunta Ekadashi is the busiest day. Confirm current timings before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Anbil lies on the northern bank of the Kollidam, east of Lalgudi, roughly 30 km from Tiruchirappalli. Tiruchirappalli Junction (and Lalgudi station on the line nearby) and Tiruchirappalli International Airport are the nearest gateways; the last stretch is by road, and local buses and taxis serve the village.
